info.bio:
Richard Steven Valenzuela (Ritchie Valens) nació el 13 de mayo de 1941 y murió el 3 de febrero de 1959 en un accidente aéreo en Iowa. Este famoso cantante, guitarrista y pionero del Rock americano nació en Los Ángeles (California) y toda su familia era de origen mexicano.

Su corta carrera, sólo duraría unos 8 meses, fue truncada a los 17 años por un accidente de aviación, pero ese tiempo le bastó sin embargo, para ganarse un lugar en la historia del Rock and Roll de los años 50.

scenes.name: The Velvet Underground y el Exploding Plastic Inevitable
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Lou Reed quería llevar al pop la mirada sin concesiones de Burroughs, Purdy y Selby (heroína, prostitución masculina, vida gay y travesti) y amaba el doo-wop, el R&B profundo y el «Sally Go Round the Roses» de las Jaynetts: para él la música era «la única cosa viva». John Cale venía del Dream Syndicate de La Monte Young, con sus drones meditativos; Reed ya había grabado una obra maestra del dron de una nota, «The Ostrich». Tocaban delante de películas en la Cinematheque de Jonas Mekas cuando Warhol los adoptó a finales de 1965 y Paul Morrissey les impuso como cantante a Nico, la «Pop Girl» de 1966. Su carta de presentación fue tocar ante 350 psiquiatras («un tratamiento de electroshock»); después vinieron Uptight y el Exploding Plastic Inevitable en el Dom de St Mark’s Place (abril): luces, estroboscopios, Screen Tests, bola de espejos, la danza sadomaso de Malanga y Woronov y drones a un volumen insoportable. En California chocaron con la escena local («ellos iban de ácido, nosotros de anfetamina»; Gleason los llamó camp y enfermos). Su primer single en Verve, de Tom Wilson, «All Tomorrow’s Parties» / «I’ll Be Your Mirror» (julio), un producto pop art total, no tuvo ni reseñas ni radio. Eran un espejo de la América de 1966 que casi nadie quiso mirar.

scenes.name: Rock'n'roll
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Fusión de rhythm'n'blues y country, con mucho más peso del primero. Chuck Berry inventa en 1955 el rock'n'roll tal como se conocerá durante cincuenta años (la guitarra como instrumento protagonista, canciones propias que hablan a los adolescentes); Bo Diddley aporta el ritmo «hambone», Little Richard y Esquerita el histerismo y el maquillaje (el primer «decadence-rock»), Jerry Lee Lewis el piano feroz y Sun Records el rockabilly. Elvis Presley es, para Scaruffi, «la primera gran estafa del rock'n'roll». Buddy Holly y Eddie Cochran abren otra vía; en paralelo nacen el soul (Ray Charles), la exótica (Martin Denny, Esquivel), la música electrónica de cinta y, en Gran Bretaña, el skiffle.

podcast.title: Death in Plane Crash (1959)
podcast.body: Richie Valens died in a plane crash on February 3, 1959, along with Buddy Holly and The Big Bopper, while traveling during the "Winter Dance Party" tour. He had been suffering from the flu during the miserable tour conditions and took Buddy Holly's chartered plane for comfort. "You're likely also to know that Richie Valens and the Big Bopper died in the same crash, even if you don't know any of the songs that either of those two artists recorded."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Death in Plane Crash (1959)
podcast.body: Valens died in a plane crash in 1959, alongside Buddy Holly and The Big Bopper. This tragedy deprived music of where he might have taken Latin rock, as he was proud to be Mexican and a significant influence on later artists like Carlos Santana. "His death in that plane crash with Buddy Holly and the Big Bopper in 1959 was tragic on many levels. One of those being that had deprived us of where he might have taken Latin rock."

podcast.title: Last-Minute Plane Passenger (1959)
podcast.body: Valens was offered a seat on Buddy Holly's chartered plane to Fargo, North Dakota, given the harsh tour conditions and his illness, replacing Tommy Allsup or Waylon Jennings. "eventually they gave up their seats to the two other people who were suffering the most, the big bumper and valence."

podcast.title: Plane Crash Death (1959)
podcast.body: Ritchie Valens was killed in a small plane crash in a cornfield outside Mason City, Iowa, on February 3, 1959. This tragedy, which also claimed the lives of Buddy Holly and Big Wopper, is historically referred to as "the day the music died." "Buddy Holly, Richie Val, and Big Wopper were all killed when their small plane went down in a cornfield outside of Mason City, Iowa."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Taking Turns Drumming (1959)
podcast.body: During the Winter Dance Party tour, after drummer Carl Bunch was hospitalized with frostbite, Richie Valens, along with Buddy Holly and Dion, took turns playing drums for three days as they were all adequate drummers. "Holly, Dion and Valens would all take it in turns playing the drums, as all of them were adequate drummers."

podcast.title: "Little Richard of the Valley" Nickname
podcast.body: Before his career direction was shaped by Bob Keane, Valens was primarily perceived as an R&B singer. This perception earned him the nickname "the Little Richard of the Valley," highlighting his vocal and performance style's similarity to the renowned R&B artist. "he was being referred to as the little Richard of the Valley."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Appearance in "Go Johnny Go" Film
podcast.body: Richie Valens featured in the 1959 Alan Freed film "Go Johnny Go," where he performed his song "Ooh My Head" and appeared in several other scenes. However, he was given no spoken lines, as the film's structure stipulated that musical performers were compensated solely as a form of promotion, while anyone delivering dialogue was classified as an actor and required separate payment. The film also showcased other notable artists including Chuck Berry, Eddie Cochran, The Flamingos, and Jackie Wilson. "Valens performed Oomai Head, and also appeared in several scenes of the film, but had no lines as the musical performers were being paid, as the film was considered to be promotion for them, while anyone who had a line was considered an actor and had to be paid."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Biopic Influence on Derek Whibley
podcast.body: The 1987 movie "La Bamba," which tells the story of Ritchie Valens, deeply moved a seven-year-old Derek Whibley and inspired him to want to play the guitar. "the Richie Valin's story and that was I think in 87 so I would have been seven and I just fell in love with that movie and I just thought I want to play guitar."

podcast.title: Death Before Film Release
podcast.body: Ritchie Valens was featured in the 1959 film "Go Johnny Go," but tragically, he was already deceased by the time the film was released. This made the movie a poignant "last gasp of rock and roll cultural relevance" for him. "By the time the film had come out, Valenz was already dead."

podcast.title: Delayed Audition with Bob Keane
podcast.body: Valens' initial audition with Bob Keane was postponed because, at the time Machia arrived to take him, Valens was at home minding his siblings. He had to wait for his mother's return before he could leave for the studio. "Valencia was minding the other children at home, and had to wait until his mother got back before he could go to the studio."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Unpopularity and Appearance
podcast.body: Richie Valens experienced some unpopularity among other Mexican Americans at his school, partly due to his physical appearance. He was notably light-skinned, which played into existing colorism among Latino youths in the area, and was also described as quite fat. Additionally, his willingness to associate with individuals of other races, including Black and White friends, set him apart from some of his peers. "Some of this was to do with his appearance. He was notably light-skinned from Mexican American, and apparently there was a level of colorism among Latino kids in that area at that time, and he was also quite fat."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Guitar Playing Limitations and Workarounds
podcast.body: Despite his natural talent and passion for the guitar, Valens was not a technically proficient guitarist when he began recording. He was limited to playing in only a few keys, mainly D or A, and typically used only three or four chords. When a song required the key of D flat, he would manually tune his guitar down a half step as he didn't know the chords for that key. On another occasion, he expressed frustration when trying to guide a bass player for a session, as the low D part he heard in his head was beyond the bass guitar's lowest E note. "Valencia was not a particularly profession guitarist. He had a lot of natural skill and a love of the instrument, but when he first started recording, he could only play in a handful of keys."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Ill-fated Tour
podcast.body: Richie Valens performed on the penultimate date of an ill-fated tour, which was attended by a young Robert Zimmerman (Bob Dylan), alongside Buddy Holly and The Big Bopper. "He was enough of a fan of Rock and Roll music that he went to see Buddy Holly, Richie Valens, and the Big Bopper, on the penultimate date of their ill-fated tour."

podcast.title: Improvisational Recording Technique
podcast.body: Due to Valens' spontaneous performing style, most of his completed recordings were laboriously compiled by Bob Keane from numerous takes. Stan Ross, co-owner of Gold Star Studios, vividly described these heavily spliced tapes as appearing as if they had been "through World War XIV." Valens typically entered the studio with only a basic melody idea and a few lyrical fragments, then improvised multiple variations of the song, from which the best segments were edited together to form the final recording. "most of the recordings he completed were pulled together by Bob Keane from multiple takes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Iowa Plane Crash Fatality
podcast.body: Ritchie Valens died early in 1959 in an infamous Iowa plane crash, an event that also claimed the lives of J.P. Richardson (The Big Bopper) and Buddy Holly. "that also took the lives of Buddy Holly and Richie Valens."

podcast.title: Lyrical and Musical Spontaneity
podcast.body: Members of The Silhouette frequently observed Valens' stage performances, where he would begin playing a song, such as Little Richard's "Jenny Jenny," but after only a few lines, he would start improvising entirely new melodies and lyrics that were unique to each performance. This spontaneous approach supports Bob Keane's assertion that Valens typically brought only a four or eight-bar riff and a few lines of lyrics to sessions, improvising the rest for Keane to later shape and structure. "he would start out playing, for example, Jenny Jenny by little Richard, but after a few lines he would start improvising his own new melody and lyrics, which would be different every time."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Mexican Heritage
podcast.body: Richie Valens was very proud of his Mexican heritage, and it's speculated that had he survived, he might have recorded as a rock star in Spanish. "Richie Valens was very proud to be Mexican, so it would have been interesting to see what his career arc would have been had he survived."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 25 - The Hispanic Influence on 70s Popular Music

podcast.title: Mortgage Fundraiser Performance
podcast.body: In January 1958, The Silhouette, Valens' band, organized and played a self-promoted show in a rented hall. The primary purpose of this concert was to raise money specifically to cover Valens' family's mortgage payment for that particular month. "In a hole they'd rented out in order to raise money to pay for Valencia's family's mortgage payment for that month."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Name Change from Ricardo Valenzuela
podcast.body: Richie Valens changed his name from Ricardo Valenzuela to get his records played on the radio, at the suggestion of his manager. "He had to change his name to get his record played on the radio."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 25 - The Hispanic Influence on 70s Popular Music

podcast.title: Signed for Energy, Not Skill
podcast.body: Bob Keane decided to sign Valens to a record deal primarily because he was impressed by Valens' raw energy during his audition, rather than his established musical ability. Following the signing, Keane took on the role of shaping Valens into a new style of performer. "Keane was impressed with Valencia, not because of his ability, but because of his energy."
